summary: Applies random single-character, three-character and token-level mutations (18 per token position) to CWEval prompts and shows that such tiny, benign perturbations frequently flip generated code between secure and vulnerable for three open code LLMs (CodeLlama-70B, DeepSeek-Coder-33B, Qwen3-Coder-30B) across C, C++, Go, JS and Python. Linear/MLP probes on the prompt-end hidden state predict joint functional+secure outcome with mean AUC ~0.70, higher for input-handling CWEs (0.753) than secure-defaults CWEs (0.674).

claims.claim: Mutations as small as one character can flip generated code from secure to vulnerable, with more harm than improvement.
claims.evidence: Figures 1-2 (fraction of CWEs affected by >=10 mutations; mean fraction of flipping mutations), Fig. 5 worked example (tar path-traversal guard dropped, DeepSeek-Coder-33B CWE-022). Per-mutation tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction (Appendix A). Stability at T=0 checked with three samples: 2/324 non-uniform (§4.1).

claims.claim: Mid-prompt (docstring/spec) mutations are most harmful; for most positions only a few of 18 mutation variants matter.
Input-handling vulnerabilities are more predictable from prompt hidden states (mean AUC 0.753) than secure-defaults ones (0.674).
claims.evidence: Table 3: 9 vs 9 CWEs, bootstrap 95% CI ±0.038/±0.037, one-sided Mann-Whitney U=68, p=0.009; numbers match abstract. But the two families were labelled manually and introduced after observing where high/low AUCs cluster (§4.4; acknowledged in Limitations), only 18 CWEs clear the 10%-flip threshold, and the functional-target replication (Table 6) uses a different 11/8 split.

claims.claim: Effects hold across model families and sizes.
claims.evidence: Appendix A.2 with gpt-oss-120B and Qwen2.5-Coder-3B; Table 4 baselines; qualitative comparison of figures only.

patterns.note: Indirect: security of generated code is fragile to ordinary prompt variation, so deterministic post-generation security checks (SAST/tests) are needed rather than trusting prompt wording.
CWEval's paired functional+security test oracles are what expose the flips; execution-based oracles are the measurement instrument.
Explicitly frames the threat model as beyond prompt injection: benign typos, not adversarial input.
Mutations in the spec/docstring portion of the prompt are the most harmful (§4.3): spec wording precision matters, but small spec edits alone can change security outcomes.

methodology.sample: CWEval tasks across 5 languages (20/21/19/23/25 CWEs per language; 108 CWE-language cells per model), 18 mutations per token position; probes on cells where >=10% of mutations flip the label.
methodology.baselines: Unmutated prompt as baseline; no comparison to prior robustness methods (none target security).
methodology.models: CodeLlama-70B, DeepSeek-Coder-33B, Qwen3-Coder-30B; appendix gpt-oss-120B, Qwen2.5-Coder-3B. No closed frontier models.
methodology.variance: T=0 with 3-sample stability check; T=0.8 sensitivity in App. A.3; BH-corrected tests; bootstrap CIs on group AUC means.
methodology.ablations: Mutation type, position, temperature, model family/size; probe family/layer sweep (App. C).
methodology.contamination_controls: None discussed for CWEval; less critical since relative change vs original prompt is measured.
methodology.languages: C, C++, Go, JavaScript, Python; no Java.

standards.artifacts: Code released (Apache-2.0) at an anonymous 4open.science repository (§1).

biases.detail: Input-handling vs secure-defaults families were labelled manually after observing AUC clusters; significance test is on the same data that defined the split.
CWEval single-function generation tasks, not agentic multi-file edits; perturbations are random character noise ('otherwiseV') rather than realistic paraphrase.
Probe AUC ~0.70 is presented as a usable pre-generation signal, but no detector operating point, false-positive rate, or cost is evaluated.
Only open 3B-120B models; results may not transfer to hosted frontier models used by agent hosts (acknowledged).

coi.affiliations: HES-SO Valais (IEM) and Cyber-Defence Campus, armasuisse Science and Technology (Swiss federal).

verdict_reason: Mutation-sensitivity finding is well supported (multiple models/languages, multiple-testing correction, temperature sensitivity, released code). The probing claim is weaker: post-hoc manual CWE grouping on 18 CWEs, no Java, no frontier models, single-function tasks rather than agent loops.
applicability: For a Java services/delivery team using agents across mixed hosts: do not rely on careful prompt or spec wording to get secure code; small wording differences between hosts' system prompts, AGENTS.md copies, or spec files can flip input-validation/sanitization behavior (highly relevant for cross-repository work of untrusted documents, path handling, XML/XPath parsing). Gate agent output with deterministic security checks (Semgrep/SpotBugs-FindSecBugs, security unit tests for path traversal, XXE, injection) in each of the several repositories. Hidden-state probes are not actionable with hosted models. Java was not tested, so the per-language magnitudes do not transfer.
